clean_story:
Unseen influences. Quantum completeness questioned.

The name hidden variable theories comes from the idea that tiny, unseen factors might control what we see in quantum experiments, like invisible strings pulling the puppets. Quantum mechanics says particles behave randomly until measured. Hidden variable theories say this randomness is an illusion caused by missing information. Imagine flipping a coin but not seeing the thumb pressing one side—it looks random, but the outcome was set all along. In 1935, Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen argued quantum mechanics was incomplete because it ignored these hidden controls. John Bell later designed a test: if hidden variables exist, certain particle pairs would show coordinated behavior beyond chance. Experiments since the 1970s, like Alain Aspect’s, found no evidence of these variables, supporting quantum randomness. Yet some theories, like Bohmian mechanics, still propose hidden variables guiding particles along precise paths. Three related subjects are quantum entanglement, Bell's theorem and local realism.
